lesson.title: Tener Expressions: hambre, sed & razón
lesson.subtitle: Possessing physical states with tener: tener hambre (f-→h- famine), tener sed, tener frío/calor, and tener razón ('to be right')

hook.title: Why You Are Not 'Hungry' or 'Right' — You Have Hunger and Reason!
hook.content:
In English, you say 'I am hungry, I am thirsty, I am cold, I am right' using adjectives after 'to be'. In Spanish (just like French avoir faim), these are NOUNS that you possess with tener:
• tener hambre = 'to be hungry' (lit. 'to have hunger' — notice Latin faminem shifted initial f- to silent h- in hambre, cousin of English famine!)
• tener sed = 'to be thirsty' (lit. 'to have thirst')
• tener frío = 'to be/feel cold' (for a person!)
• tener razón = 'to be right' (lit. 'to have reason')!

footnotes.title: Why 'El Hambre' Takes 'Mucha' (Just Like 'El Agua Fría')
footnotes.content: Just like el agua, hambre starts with a stressed /a/ sound (even though a silent h is written in front!), so singular 'the hunger' is el hambre — yet the word is 100% feminine, which is why we say mucha hambre!

pattern.title: Why We Say 'Tengo Mucha Hambre' (Not *Muy Hambre)!
pattern.content: Because hambre ('hunger'), sed ('thirst'), frío ('cold'), and razón ('reason') are NOUNS rather than adjectives, how do you say 'I am VERY hungry'? You cannot use muy ('very'); you must say 'I have MUCH hunger' using mucho/mucha: Tengo mucha hambre, Tengo mucha sed, Tengo mucho frío, Tienes toda la razón!
pattern.trap_note: Wait: if a PERSON feels cold, say Tengo frío ('I have cold'). If the WATER is cold, say El agua está fría (state of an object)!

exercises.prompt: Match each English expression with its Spanish partner:

matching_pairs.english: I am very hungry (much hunger, fem.)
are you thirsty? (do you have thirst?)

exercises.target_answer: tengo hambre, tengo mucha hambre, ¿tienes sed?, tienes razón, tengo frío
exercises.meaning: I am hungry (I have hunger), I am very hungry (much hunger, fem.), are you thirsty? (do you have thirst?), you are right (you have reason), I feel cold (I have cold)
exercises.explanation: Physical sensations and 'being right' are nouns possessed with tener.

exercises.prompt: Spanish el/la hambre ('hunger', from Latin faminem with f- → silent h-) shares its root with which English word for extreme food scarcity?
exercises.meaning: hambre and famine are the exact same Latin root (f- → silent h-)!
exercises.explanation: Latin famēs / faminem kept initial f- in English famine and turned f- into silent h- in Spanish hambre.

exercises.prompt: Because 'hambre' and 'sed' are feminine nouns ('hunger', 'thirst'), how do you say 'I am very hungry'?
exercises.explanation: Before a feminine noun, Spanish uses mucha ('much/a lot of'): Tengo mucha hambre.

exercises.meaning: You are right (lit. You have reason)
exercises.explanation: Tienes razón — 'to be right' is tener razón.

exercises.idea: ask a friend if they are hungry and thirsty
cues: hunger and thirst → hambre y sed?
idea_parts: hunger and thirst → hambre y sed
exercises.explanation: ¿Tienes hambre y sed? — one tienes governs both nouns.

diagnosis.cue: Hunger and thirst are nouns held with tener: ¿Tienes hambre y sed?

summary.outcome: Express hunger (tener hambre), thirst (tener sed), feeling cold (tener frío), and being right (tener razón) with tener + mucho/mucha.

use_example.german: Tienes razón — tengo mucha hambre y mucha sed.
use_example.english: You are right — I am very hungry and very thirsty.

summary.takeaway: Because hambre, sed, frío, and razón are nouns, pair them with tener and intensify them with mucho/mucha (never muy)!
summary.curiosity_teaser: Up next ([16] Days, Months & Dates): see how the seven Roman planets name the Spanish days of the week.

twist.explanation: la sed is feminine, so 'very thirsty' is Tengo mucha sed ('I have much thirst').

hambre.context_translation: I am very hungry (lit. I have much hunger).
hambre.etymology_derivation: Feminine noun (mucha hambre) that takes el in the singular like el agua, and shows f- → h- from Latin famēs!

razón.context_translation: You are completely right (lit. You have all the reason).
razón.etymology_derivation: To be right in Spanish is to 'have reason': tienes razón.

frío.etymology_derivation: Notice feminine fría agrees with el agua!

tiempo.etymology_derivation: Covers both clock/calendar time and the weather.

mucho.context_translation: Thank you very much (lit. Many graces).
mucho.etymology_derivation: muy ('very') goes before adjectives/adverbs; mucho/a/os/as goes with verbs and nouns!

tener.etymology_derivation: Latin tenēre ('to hold'). While other tongues used 'have' (like French avoir), Spanish promoted 'hold' (tener) to main possession.

tengo.etymology_derivation: Latin teneō developed an epenthetic velar g: tengo.

tienes.etymology_derivation: Stem vowel e diphthongizes to ie when stressed: tienes.

tiene.etymology_derivation: Stem change e → ie under stress.

f_to_h.name: Latin F- ➔ Silent H-
f_to_h.phonetic_rule: Latin initial f- weakened into an aspiration and became completely silent h- in Spanish, while English kept the Latin f- cognate.
f_to_h.historical_linguistics: Castilian contact with Basque/Cantabrian substrate languages lacking initial /f/ caused Latin /f-/ to weaken into silent h-.
f_to_h.philological_note: Hacer ↔ fact/manufacture; hijo ↔ filial; hierro ↔ ferrous; horno ↔ furnace. When you see a silent h-, think f.
